what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: The delegation record: RiskMandate's go-to-market plan, one workflow from an existing rule to evidence that survives change.
sections.para: Deliver one chain: existing requirement, approved delegation, implemented control, observed result, evidence after change. The product is a six-part delegation record. Translate human rules explicitly and never learn the baseline from behaviour. Three stages, a small first customer, and pilot zero on our own inbox, where Gmail cannot enforce draft-but-never-send.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Seven lines: one chain, the record, translation, an approved baseline, three stages, a small first customer, pilot zero.
sections.para: Deliver the chain once. Sell a six-part record a customer can act on. A people rule needs extracting, its ambiguities listed and the delegation approved. Behaviour is evaluated, never adopted as the baseline. Immediate value, maintenance value, repeatability. One workflow, owner and environment. Start with our inbox.

sections.label: From strategy to delivery
sections.line: From strategy to delivery: the review asks whether we can deliver one useful result, and that is the plan.
sections.para: After three rounds of AI-assisted review, the recommendation is to complete one chain from an existing requirement to evidence valid after change. That is the go-to-market plan, with one caution: an AI review agreeing with a refined position is not market validation; only a customer's decision is.

sections.label: The delegation record
sections.line: The delegation record: business requirement, agent delegation, control mapping, evidence, remaining gaps, change conditions.
sections.para: It answers what a buyer gets at the end, and is the practical coverage explanation. The behaviour policy holds the delegation and barriers; the five published states, defined to verified, become the evidence when each says what was tested and where. We sell the record and charge for keeping it true.

sections.label: A rule for people is not yet a delegation
sections.line: A rule for people is not yet a delegation to an agent: extract it, list the ambiguities, approve the delegation.
sections.para: Refunds up to £100 raise new questions: execute or recommend, what sets the amount, limits across runs, who approves exceptions and for what, which record proves eligibility, what forces re-approval. The milestones already treat correction as elicitation; the approval becomes an explicit checkpoint, and a model's interpretation never inherits the policy's authority.

sections.label: The rules we keep
sections.line: Rules kept from day one: an approved baseline, obligations as well as permissions, and precedent that needs its own approval.
sections.para: Repeated behaviour never becomes the norm, and a new permission is not new authority. Blocking every refund respects limits but fails the process, so legitimate work is measured. Approving one exception is not approving a class: generalisation needs matching facts, exclusions, an approver, scope, duration and withdrawal.

sections.label: Three stages
sections.line: Three stages: immediate value, maintenance value and repeatability, each testing a different claim.
sections.para: Fix one consequential mismatch and prove it from the protected system's record. Make a controlled change and show the affected requirement found and the retest triggered. Repeat on a related workflow or customer, measuring reuse and upkeep, and ask who pays. The evidence decides between service, software-assisted service and product.

sections.label: The first customer
sections.line: The first customer: one workflow, owner and environment, with an agent at work, a concern, controls, an owner and an engineer.
sections.para: A few consequential requirements and one working control change, with what remains uncovered stated. A second enforcement target comes later. Teams lacking controls need a different offer, cost and buyer, but not the first one.

sections.label: Pilot zero: our own inbox
sections.line: Pilot zero is our own inbox: the agent drafts and I send, and Gmail has no permission to draft without sending.
sections.para: Drafting needs gmail.compose, gmail.modify or full access, and Google describes each as allowing sending. So the mailbox cannot keep the rule. Candidate controls are a harness hook refusing sends, a setting, or drafts kept in a vault. Evidence: a send attempted and Gmail's record that nothing left; until then, an accepted expectation.

sections.label: The brief for the RiskMandate sites
sections.line: The brief for the RiskMandate sites: lead with the record, a dated capability table, the translation step, the stages.
sections.para: Lead with the delegation record rather than real-time enforcement; publish a dated table of artefacts, demonstrations, pilots, capabilities and plans, naming what stops each action; add the translation step to the milestones; add the three stages, the first-customer profile and the six-part template, with pilot zero as the first worked example.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Nothing delivered yet; the review is AI-assisted; the Gmail finding is from documentation; controls untested; the customer is a profile.
sections.para: No row of pilot zero's record is tested. An AI review's agreement is not validation. Google's scope descriptions were read on 22 October 2026, not tested. A hook is a setting and drafts outside Gmail change the workflow. We are still looking for the first customer.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: The third round of the AI-assisted review, Google's Gmail scope documentation, and our related articles.
sections.para: The review written in a ChatGPT session on 22 October 2026, paraphrased; Google's documentation of Gmail API scopes and drafts.create; and approved business mandates, drift, answering a draft, three decisions mapped, case law for agents and our first customers.
